abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel categorical framework for model-driven engineering that fundamentally reconceptualizes how software models are composed, transformed, and verified. Traditional approaches treat model transformations as functions or relations, limiting their expressiveness for capturing complex architectural patterns. We propose the Category of Modeling Architectures (CMA), where models, transformations, and properties form objects and morphisms within a unified mathematical structure. This framework enables the formal characterization of model refinement, traceability, and behavioral preservation through universal constructions. Our key contribution is demonstrating that well-known model operations—including UML class diagram extensions, state machine compositions, and domain-specific language embeddings—naturally correspond to categorical limits, colimits, and adjunctions. We establish equivalence between semantic anchoring in existing methodologies and our functorial semantics, thereby bridging model-driven engineering with advanced theoretical computer science. The CMA framework provides a foundation for automated reasoning about model correctness and transformation confluence that transcends current graph-based formalisms. A case study on cyber-physical systems modeling validates the framework's applicability to industrial-scale problems, showing how categorical abstractions enable reasoning about heterogeneous model integration that is intractable under conventional approaches.

Existing approaches to model verification suffer from the state explosion problem when analyzing software architecture models with concurrent behaviors. This paper presents a symbolic model checking technique optimized for UML composite structure diagrams and their associated state machines. Our method exploits the compositional nature of architecture models by verifying component behaviors independently before checking interaction protocols through assume-guarantee reasoning. We introduce architectural contracts—formal specifications that capture component interfaces and interaction constraints—which enable automatic generation of verification conditions. The core improvement lies in our symbolic encoding that represents model states using Ordered Decision Diagrams (ODDs) instead of traditional BDDs, reducing memory consumption by up to 60% for industrial architecture models. We formally prove the soundness of our assume-guarantee decomposition and establish completeness conditions for the contract-based verification process. Experimental evaluation on twelve architecture models from embedded systems domains demonstrates that our technique verifies properties that are intractable for existing model checkers while maintaining precision comparable to exhaustive state-space exploration. The approach significantly reduces verification time for large-scale models, enabling practical application of formal verification to model-based development workflows.

We present MetaForge, a novel integrated development environment that fundamentally changes how engineers create, validate, and evolve domain-specific modeling languages. Unlike existing tools that treat metamodeling as a secondary concern, MetaForge places language design at the core of the development workflow through a reflexive metamodeling architecture. The system implements a reflective infrastructure where the abstract syntax, concrete syntax, and semantic domains of modeling languages are uniformly represented as first-class model elements, enabling engineers to manipulate language constructs through the same mechanisms used for application models. MetaForge introduces semantic anchoring through a configurable interpretation framework that supports multiple execution semantics for the same syntax, eliminating the traditional distinction between concrete and abstract syntax layers. The tool supports collaborative language evolution through versioned metamodels with automatic migration of conforming models. A prototype implementation demonstrates the creation of three industrially-relevant DSLs for financial systems, IoT device coordination, and business process modeling. Performance evaluation shows that reflexive operations incur less than 8% overhead compared to specialized implementations while providing unprecedented flexibility for language experimentation and extension.

This paper presents TrafoBench 2.0, an advanced benchmarking framework for evaluating and comparing model transformation engines. While existing benchmarks provide synthetic workloads, they fail to capture the characteristics of real-world transformations that development teams encounter. TrafoBench 2.0 introduces a comprehensive benchmark suite comprising 47 transformation scenarios extracted from open-source projects, categorized by complexity metrics including rule count, pattern matching depth, and output size growth rate. The framework implements a novel execution environment that ensures reproducible performance measurements across different transformation engines, addressing the variability introduced by JVM warm-up, garbage collection, and filesystem caching. We significantly improve upon the original TrafoBench by incorporating hybrid workload generation that combines deterministic transformation sequences with randomized model generation, enabling assessment of engine behavior under stress conditions. The system provides automated statistical analysis with significance testing to determine whether observed performance differences are meaningful. Evaluation across five transformation engines—including Henshin, ATL, and модЕЛ—reveals previously undocumented performance characteristics and identifies optimization opportunities in current implementations. TrafoBench 2.0 is publicly available and supports community contribution of transformation scenarios.
